title: How long a borrow lasts
summary: A borrow ends at its last USE, not at the closing brace — so statement order is a tool.
lecture: Since non-lexical lifetimes (NLL), the compiler tracks where a reference is last *used*, not where it goes out of scope. A `let preview = &data;` whose final use is on the next line stops borrowing right there — later mutation or moving of `data` is fine.

This turns statement ordering into a first-class fix. 'Cannot move out of `x` because it is borrowed' or 'cannot borrow as mutable' often disappears if you finish all reads before the move or mutation — same statements, different order.
The reflex to train: when the borrow checker complains about overlap, don't reach for clone — first ask whether the timeline can be untangled.

example.caption: Borrow, finish using it, then move. Order is the fix.
